title: Subnets and VLSM: How to Calculate Fast
lead: The magic number, subnet boundaries, host counts, working backward from a requirement to a mask, and splitting a network across sites of different sizes.

sections.title: The one table you need to memorize

blocks.text: Everything comes down to powers of two. Learn one column — the "magic number" — and the rest follows:
**Magic number = 256 − the mask's value in that octet.** Subnets step through in increments of this number, starting at zero.
For shorter masks, the same logic works in the third octet:

blocks.title: Remember
paras: Hosts = `2^h − 2` (h = host bits). Subnets from a given network = `2^s` (s = the number of bits "borrowed" from the host part). There's no "minus two" for subnets on the modern exam.

sections.title: Finding the network and broadcast address in 20 seconds

blocks.text: Problem: **172.16.77.100/26** — which subnet, and where are the boundaries?

items: Boundaries in the fourth octet are multiples of 64: 0, 64, 128, 192.
100 falls in the block **64…127**.
So: network `172.16.77.64`, broadcast `172.16.77.127`, usable addresses `.65 – .126`.

blocks.text: The same algorithm works for any mask. If the octet of interest isn't the last one, do the math in that octet: for `/20` (255.255.**240**.0), the magic number is 16, so blocks step 0, 16, 32, 48… in the third octet, while the fourth octet runs from 0 to 255.
Example: **10.5.36.200/20**. Third-octet blocks: 32 and 48; 36 falls into the 32 block. Network `10.5.32.0`, broadcast `10.5.47.255`, hosts `10.5.32.1 – 10.5.47.254`.
Five more worked problems
Work through these until the answer comes to you before you finish reading the question. On the exam, this type of question should take under a minute.

**1. 192.168.100.164/27 — network, broadcast, range.** Mask 224 → magic number 32. Boundaries: 0, 32, 64, 96, 128, 160, 192, 224. 164 falls between 160 and 191. Answer: network `192.168.100.160`, broadcast `.191`, hosts `.161 – .190`.

**2. Which address can't be assigned to a host in 10.20.30.0/29?** Magic number 8, blocks 0–7, 8–15, 16–23… In the 0–7 block, neither `.0` (network) nor `.7` (broadcast) is valid. If `10.20.30.8` shows up among the choices, it's actually valid — but it's in the **next** subnet.
**3. How many /30 subnets fit in 172.16.4.0/22, and how many addresses is that?** A /22 holds `2^(30−22) = 256` /30 subnets. Total addresses in the /22 is 1024, and each /30 has four.

**4. Two interfaces: 192.168.1.62/26 and 192.168.1.65/26. Are they in the same subnet?** Magic number 64. The first is in the 0–63 block, the second in the 64–127 block. **No**, these are different subnets — exactly the kind of question that shows up in the question bank as "why don't these hosts see each other even though the addresses are next to each other."

**5. Given the mask 255.255.255.248 and the address 10.0.0.44, where does traffic to 10.0.0.47 end up?** Magic number 8, block 40–47. The address `.47` is the **broadcast** of this subnet, not a host. A ping to it will get replies from every host on the segment, and it can't be assigned to an interface.
Table: how many hosts — which mask
Working backward is common enough that it's worth memorizing the right-hand column directly:

sections.title: The reverse problem: which mask is needed

blocks.text: Asked for "a subnet for 50 hosts":

items: Find the nearest power of two that's ≥ 50 + 2 = 52 → that's 64 (`2^6`).
So 6 host bits → 32 − 6 = **/26**.

blocks.text: Asked to "split a /24 into 8 subnets":

items: 24 + 3 = **/27**, with 30 hosts in each.

blocks.title: Trap
paras: "For 62 hosts" is `/26` (62 = 64−2), but "for 63 hosts" is already `/25`. Always check whether the requirement still fits after subtracting the two reserved addresses — this boundary is where most points get lost.

sections.title: VLSM: different masks within one network

blocks.text: A classic problem: given `192.168.1.0/24`, allocate space for sites needing 100, 50, and 25 hosts, plus three point-to-point links.
One rule: **biggest blocks first, then smaller ones**, or you'll end up with gaps.

The remaining `192.168.1.236 – 255` is free for future growth. If you started with the /30 links first, the large LAN might not fit into a contiguous block — that's exactly the point of the ordering rule.
For links between routers, use a **/30** (2 hosts) or **/31** (RFC 3021, both addresses usable); spending a /24 on two addresses is a classic wrong answer in efficiency questions.
The reverse operation: combining several networks under one prefix.

items: Convert the third octet to binary: 00000000, 00000001, 00000010, 00000011.
Six high-order bits match across all four.

blocks.text: Rule of thumb: however many consecutive networks you're summarizing, that power of two is how many bits shorter the prefix gets (4 networks = 2 bits = /24 → /22). The summary block must start on an address that's a multiple of its own size: 10.1.0.0/22 works, 10.1.1.0/22 doesn't.

sections.title: Binary notation, for when the magic number doesn't help

blocks.text: Sometimes it's faster to just look at the bits — for example, to explain to yourself why `192.168.1.62/26` and `192.168.1.65/26` are in different subnets.

62  = 00111110  ┐ first two bits 00 → block 0
   65  = 01000001  ┘ first two bits 01 → block 64
        └┬┘
         these 2 bits are taken from the host part by the /26 mask

A /26 mask takes the two high-order bits of the last octet for the subnet number. If those bits match, the addresses are in the same subnet; if not, they're in different ones. The same technique answers "which part of the address determines the network."
It helps to remember the bit values in an octet: `128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1`. The mask is ones on the left:
ACLs and OSPF use an **inverted** mask: where the mask has a 1, the wildcard has a 0.
Computed by subtracting each octet from 255. A wildcard of `0.0.0.0` means exactly one address, `255.255.255.255` means any address.

sections.title: Working through a typical exhibit-based question

blocks.text: Asked: which subnet is this, and does 10.10.13.200 fall within it?

items: The mask is /25, magic number 128 → blocks 0–127 and 128–255.
The host is in block **10.10.13.0/25**, usable .1–.126, broadcast .127.

Address .200 falls in a **different** subnet (10.10.13.128/25) — traffic to it would go through the gateway, not directly. If the gateway itself were set to .200, the host wouldn't be able to reach outside its network at all.

sections.title: Diagnostic: a subnet "suddenly" runs out of addresses

blocks.text: **Symptom.** In a 40-person office, new laptops stop getting an IP from DHCP, even though everything used to work fine; users already connected are unaffected.
**What to check.** Subnet size against the actual number of devices:

R1# show ip dhcp pool OFFICE
Pool OFFICE :
 Utilization mark (high/low)    : 100 / 0
 Subnet size (first/last)       : 0 / 0
 Total addresses                : 62
 Leased addresses               : 62
 Excluded addresses             : 6

**What it means.** `Leased` equals `Total` — the pool is completely exhausted. The subnet was cut as a `/26` (62 hosts) with headroom for an original 40 people, but over time IP phones, printers, access points, and guest devices were added — each one taking a separate address from the same pool. Exam takeaway: **VLSM is sized by the number of IP consumers, not the number of people**, and if that's not accounted for with headroom, a subnet designed too tightly will eventually hit a wall — and expanding a `/26` to a `/25` without recalculating the neighboring blocks (see the "biggest blocks first" rule from the VLSM section) isn't possible on a live network if the next block is already taken by a link or another LAN.

sections.title: Working a full combined VLSM problem

blocks.text: Given: `10.20.0.0/22` (1024 addresses), needing to fit: a headquarters site with 300 hosts, a branch with 120, a warehouse with 40, and three dedicated router links connecting all three, each /30. Allocate large to small, per the VLSM rule.

**Step 1 — headquarters, 300 hosts.** Nearest power of two ≥ 302 (300+2) is 512 (`2^9`) → `/23`. Take the first /23 block whole: `10.20.0.0/23` (addresses `10.20.0.0 – 10.20.1.255`), usable hosts `10.20.0.1 – 10.20.1.254`.

**Step 2 — branch, 120 hosts.** Nearest power of two ≥ 122 is 128 (`2^7`) → `/25`. The next free address after the /23 block is `10.20.2.0`. Block `10.20.2.0/25` (`10.20.2.0 – 10.20.2.127`), hosts `10.20.2.1 – 10.20.2.126`.
**Step 3 — warehouse, 40 hosts.** Nearest power of two ≥ 42 is 64 (`2^6`) → `/26`. The next free address is `10.20.2.128`. Block `10.20.2.128/26` (`10.20.2.128 – 10.20.2.191`), hosts `.129 – .190`.
**Step 4 — three /30 links between routers.** The next free address is `10.20.2.192`. Links: `10.20.2.192/30`, `10.20.2.196/30`, `10.20.2.200/30`.
Final table:

`10.20.2.204 – 10.20.3.255` is free for growth. Had the links been allocated before the headquarters site (breaking the "biggest blocks first" order), the `/23` for headquarters would no longer fit as a single contiguous block — that's the mechanical reason for the rule, not just a convention.

items: "Which subnet and mask identify what is configured on this interface?" — worked out via the magic number.
"How many usable hosts are available in 192.168.1.0/27?" — 30.
"Which subnet mask is required for 500 hosts?" — 512 = 2^9 → /23.
"What is the broadcast address of 10.4.72.9/21?" — blocks of 8 in the third octet: network 10.4.72.0, broadcast **10.4.79.255**.
"Which summary route covers these four networks?" — the shared prefix.
Drag-and-drop: matching an address to a subnet, a mask to a host count.
"A DHCP pool shows leased addresses equal to total addresses. What is the most likely cause?" — the subnet backing the pool was cut too small for the actual number of devices.
"When performing VLSM, in which order should subnets be allocated?" — from the largest required subnet down to the smallest, or the large block may not fit contiguously.

items.q: A subnet is needed for at least 300 hosts. Which prefix?
How many /28 subnets fit in a /24, and how many hosts in each?
How do you cover 172.16.8.0/24 … 172.16.11.0/24 with a single prefix?
items.a: 172.16.8.0/22 — four networks, so the prefix is two bits shorter.

items.q: Why use a /30 for a link between routers instead of a /24?
items.a: Only two addresses are needed; a /24 wastes 254 addresses, while a /30 provides exactly two usable ones.

items.q: A DHCP pool on a /26 shows leased = total. Should you expand the pool first, or figure out the actual device count?
items.a: First count the actual number of IP consumers (not just people — phones, access points, printers); if the subnet was designed too tightly, you'll need to recalculate VLSM for the whole block, not just add a few addresses.

items.q: From 10.20.0.0/22 you need to carve out blocks for 300, 120, and 40 hosts plus three /30 links. In what order are they allocated, and why?
items.a: Largest to smallest — first the /23 for 300 hosts, then the /25 for 120, then the /26 for 40, and the /30 links last; otherwise the larger block might not find a contiguous free space for itself.
